cache.md#cache-directories-redirected-to.text:
The container redirects package-manager and other tool cache directories (an uv cache, XDG cache and data directories) to `/tmp` inside the container instead of letting them land in mounted host paths.

**Reason:** caches grow without bound and are cheap to rebuild; persisting them on the host would fill host disk with per-container cache files and create host-owned files (the root-owned-file problem the user-switch plan addresses). Keeping them in the container's own writable layer means they die with the container, which is the correct lifetime for a cache.

**Rejected alternative:** let caches write into mounted host directories. Host disk fills with stale cache files, and the files are root-owned until the user switch lands.

container-runtime.md#base-image-node-22-.text:
Both Dockerfiles use `node:22-trixie` as the base image.

**Reason:** pi >= 0.84 requires Node >= 22 — it uses `fs.globSync`, which does not exist on Node 20. Trixie is Debian stable.

**Rejected alternative:** Node 20 base image. It works until pi is invoked, then crashes; pi >= 0.84 cannot run on it at all.

**Rejected alternative:** older Debian (bookworm/bullseye). Not wrong, but trixie is what the node:22 image ships by default and nothing here needs an older userland.

container-runtime.md#container-runs-as-r.text:
The container runs as root (UID 0, GID 0). A documented plan exists to run it as a named user matching the host UID/GID so files written into mounted directories are owned correctly, but it has not been implemented.

**Reason (for the plan, confirmed):** files pi writes into bind-mounted host directories must carry the host user's UID/GID or the host user cannot manage them later. Host facts used by the plan: the host user's UID maps directly to the same container UID on macOS Docker Desktop (verified 2026-09-29); in Debian trixie GID 20 is already the existing `dialout` group, so no groupadd is needed; pi's profile directory contains relative symlinks that break if the profile is mounted at anything other than a flat path under the home directory. (The concrete UID/GID pair is recorded in `NOTES.md`, the maintainer's working notes.)

**Reason (for still being root):** unknown — no record of why the switch has not been done since the plan was written (2026-09-29).

**Considered:** the original plan (sshd as root + privilege transition in the entrypoint + marker-file ownership fix) was reviewed by three sub-agent reviewers and judged sound but over-engineered. The revised design: create the user in the Dockerfile, pass the UID/GID to `docker run`, drop all in-entrypoint privilege logic, do a one-time volume ownership migration manually, and accept that a stale working directory recorded in herdr's session state survives the switch (the user creates a new workspace). Rollback is a `docker rm -f`, a one-time ownership migration back to root, and reverting the script change.

**Why this needs an answer:** until the switch lands, everything pi writes into mounted directories is root-owned on the host, which is the exact problem the plan exists to fix; an open question about why it is still open is recorded rather than guessed (Core rule 1).

dockerfile.md#herdr-binary-pinned-by-ver.text:
The herdr binary is downloaded into the image at a pinned version with a SHA256 checksum verified at build time.

**Reason:** herdr is the state-owning component of the whole workflow; an unpinned or unverified binary would make the state format (and therefore state persistence across container rebuilds) depend on whatever the upstream server happened to serve at build time.

**Rejected alternative:** install herdr from an unpinned release URL. A herdr release that changes state format would silently break state carried in the named volume from an earlier build.

dockerfile.md#herdr-web-source-vendored-.text:
The web-UI bridge image builds from a source tarball checked into `build-context/`, with the archive's SHA256 pinned, rather than fetching herdr-web's source from its upstream at build time.

**Reason:** the bridge's source is not a versioned release the project can point at by tag; pinning a specific commit as a checksummed archive makes the build reproducible without depending on upstream's default branch staying compatible. The archive is MIT-licensed upstream, matching this project's license.

**Rejected alternative:** clone or fetch the upstream repository at image build time. The build would silently track upstream's default branch; a breaking change upstream would break the bridge image without any change in this repository.

entrypoint.md#entrypoint-removes-stale-h.text:
The entrypoint deletes any socket files left in the herdr state directory before starting the herdr server.

**Reason:** if the container was killed or crashed without a clean shutdown (SIGTERM path), herdr's socket files can remain in the (named-volume) state directory, and the next server start fails because the socket path is already taken. Removing them at start makes a crash-then-restart cycle work without manual intervention.

**Rejected alternative:** require a clean `herdr.sh down` before every restart. The whole point of the named volume is that state survives container death; a socket-cleanup requirement would turn every crash into a manual-recovery step.

**Note:** this complements, not replaces, the clean-shutdown recommendation in the herdr state entries — clean shutdown still avoids the stale-socket condition; this makes the messy path survivable.

**See:** herdr-state.md — 6351bb41-1742-4cbb-b011-11bf1a48edfa — as of 2026-10-10

herdr-cli.md#herdr-agent-prompt-no-until.text:
When driving herdr's agent-prompt command from the host and waiting for it to settle, do not add a `--until` flag for normal work; wait for the first settled idle/done/blocked state instead.

**Reason:** the wait command without `--until` accepts whichever of idle/done/blocked the agent settles into first, which is what pi does after a normal turn. Adding `--until done` (or similar) narrows the wait to one specific state; an agent that settles into idle — the normal end of a turn — is then reported as a timeout even though it finished fine.

**Rejected alternative:** use `--until done` so the wait is explicit about the expected end state. Produces false timeouts on the common path; `--until` is only for flows that genuinely need one specific state (e.g. waiting for blocked).

herdr-state.md#herdr-state-on-a-named-vo.text:
Herdr's state directory is a Docker named volume, not a bind mount from the host.

**Reason:** macOS Docker Desktop's gRPC-Fuse implementation cannot create unix domain sockets on bind mounts — `bind()` fails and the socket file cannot be removed — and herdr's server requires a socket in its state directory. A bind-mounted state directory therefore cannot work at all, not just partially.

**Rejected alternative:** bind-mount the herdr state directory from the host. Verified to fail: sockets cannot be created, and stale ones cannot be cleaned up from inside the container (socket removal returns an unsupported error on the host path).

**Rejected alternative:** bind-mount individual state files (session file, history file) from the host. Herdr persists state with an atomic rename pattern; rename-over-existing-file fails silently on macOS bind mounts. Herdr would start but never persist anything.

**Rejected alternative:** a per-project host directory mounted in, instead of one state directory. Same socket and rename failure as the first two; the named volume is the only persistence that works on this host.

herdr-state.md#herdr-state-directory-fol.text:
The container sets `HOME` and mounts the state volume at `$HOME/.config/herdr`, rather than setting `HERDR_CONFIG_DIR` to point herdr at the volume.

**Reason:** herdr 0.9.1 ignores `HERDR_CONFIG_DIR` entirely and always uses `$HOME/.config/herdr`; changing `HOME` moves the state directory, and that is honored. The mount therefore has to land exactly where herdr looks, via `HOME`.

**Rejected alternative:** set `HERDR_CONFIG_DIR` to the volume path and leave `HOME` at the default. Verified ineffective on 0.9.1; the state directory would silently resolve elsewhere.

herdr-state.md#herdr-config-self-contain.text:
`herdr-config.toml` lives in this repository and is copied into the container's state directory on first start.

**Reason:** the repository is meant to be a self-contained recipe — everything needed to reproduce the setup is in the repo, not linked to host-specific locations like a user's own herdr config directory.

**Rejected alternative:** link or mount the user's existing host herdr config into the container. It breaks the self-contained property and leaks host-specific settings into a throwaway container.

herdr-state.md#herdr-sh-down-sigterm-is-.text:
Stopping the container goes through `docker rm -f` (SIGTERM) or compose down, which lets herdr clean up its socket files before exiting.

**Reason:** herdr's server-stop command exits the server process immediately; when herdr is the container's main process the container dies without cleaning up its sockets, and a stale socket in the (named-volume) state directory then blocks the next start until it is manually deleted.

**Rejected alternative:** send the herdr server-stop API command from the host and let the container die. Leaves stale sockets behind; the clean socket cleanup only happens on SIGTERM.

herdr-state.md#session-history-json-can-.text:
Herdr's pane-history file records terminal output, which can include API keys or passwords an agent prints during a session.

**Reason:** `pane_history = true` in the container's herdr config makes herdr persist what appears in agent panes; that is by design (re-attach after a crash and see what happened), but it means sensitive output ends up in the state volume.

**Consequence:** the state volume holds anything an agent ever printed. The volume is not directly readable from the macOS host (it lives inside the Docker VM), which is a mitigation but not a guarantee — `docker cp` or a volume dump would expose it.

**Considered:** setting `pane_history = false` in the container config was recorded as an open item. Trade-off: lose the ability to see what a pane did before a crash, in exchange for not accumulating printed secrets.

host-platform.md#macos-docker-desktop-fi.text:
Several decisions in this project exist because of verified limitations of macOS Docker Desktop's gRPC-Fuse bind-mount implementation, not because they are the ideal choice in general:

- Unix domain sockets cannot be created on bind mounts, and existing socket files cannot be removed from the host side.
- Atomic file writes (rename over an existing file) silently fail on bind mounts.
- Ordinary file creation and reading/writing work fine on bind mounts.
- Docker named volumes are real Linux filesystems inside the Docker VM and have none of these limitations.

**Reason:** these behaviors were each verified directly (a failing `bind()`, a failing `unlink()` on a socket, herdr starting but never persisting state) before the workarounds were adopted, rather than assumed from documentation.

**Consequence:** the "use a named volume for anything that needs a socket or an atomic write, bind-mount only what genuinely needs to be a host path" rule in this project is specific to this host's platform. Moving to a platform without these limitations (Linux host, or a newer Docker Desktop backend) lifts several of the constraints recorded in the herdr state and mount entries — those entries' `Revisit when` conditions exist for exactly this.

**See:** herdr-state.md — 8df98718-04bf-4ac1-8b60-df6d70252503 — as of 2026-10-10

memory.md#durable-pairing-memory-is-file.text:
The project's durable pairing memory (decisions, verified findings, rejected approaches, open items) lives in committed Markdown files by type — purpose and pointers in `AGENTS.md`, user-facing workflow docs in `README.md`, verified technical findings and rejected approaches in `NOTES.md`, planned architectures in `docs/` — rather than in agent session history.

**Reason:** agent session memory does not survive across sessions, agents, or machines; a project that future agents (human or AI) will work on needs its reasoning in files that are versioned, searchable, and shared with the code. The selection test in `AGENTS.md` (future usefulness, consequence, essence, home) is the bar for what gets persisted where.

**Rejected alternative:** rely on agent session transcripts or a shared "memory" service for the project's rationale. A transcript is per-session and per-agent; a service adds a dependency the project's "self-contained, no daemon" design explicitly avoids (see the herdr state entries, which apply the same reasoning to runtime state).

**Consequence:** an agent that does work in this project and finds durable, future-useful information is expected to write it into the matching file as part of finishing the work, not at the end of the session.

mounts.md#dev-and-dev-external-mounted-r.text:
The herdr container mounts `~/dev` and `~/dev-external` read-only, at the host's own paths inside the container; specific subdirectories can be overridden read-write via an environment variable listing them.

**Reason:** the default-deny policy — the agent sees the whole development tree but cannot write to it unless a specific directory is explicitly opted in — is a stated user requirement. Mounting at the host's own paths (rather than a translated container path) means no path-translation logic in the script: the same path works on both sides.

**Rejected alternative:** mount the development directories read-write by default. The agent could corrupt or rewrite any of the host's other projects while working in one.

**Rejected alternative:** translate host paths to different container paths. Requires the agent and any tooling to know the mapping; keeping the identical path on both sides removes that class of bug.

mounts.md#the-working-repository-is-the-.text:
The repository the container works in is mounted read-write (at a well-known in-container path) and is the only writable project-content mount by default; everything else is read-only unless explicitly overridden.

**Reason:** same rationale as the read-only default — an agent working on one repository should not be able to touch the rest of the host's development tree without an explicit, per-invocation opt-in. The opt-in mechanism is the read-write override variable from the read-only-defaults entry.

multi-instance.md#each-herdr-instance-ge.text:
Running multiple herdr containers in parallel (one per repository, for parallel agent work) gives each instance its own state volume and its own host SSH port, derived deterministically from the instance name.

**Reason:** herdr's state directory contains sockets and a single coherent session; two containers cannot share one state volume. A deterministic per-name port (base port plus a hash of the name) keeps multi-instance usage from requiring the user to track which port is which.

**Rejected alternative:** one shared state volume for all instances. Herdr's server would see another instance's sockets and session state, and concurrent writes would corrupt it; each instance needs its own volume.

**Rejected alternative:** let the user assign ports manually. Works for two instances; breaks down as the number grows, since there is no way to remember which port belongs to which instance.

ollama.md#local-llm-gateway-pointed-at-t.text:
The container's local-LLM provider points its base URL at the Docker host gateway address (a `host.docker.internal` hostname with the gateway's port) instead of the host's loopback address.

**Reason:** the gateway runs on the host; inside the container, loopback is the container's own loopback, so the only way to reach a host process is through Docker's host-gateway hostname. The provider name was likewise set to a custom value matching the gateway's configuration.

**Consequence:** this is untested end-to-end (the gateway was down when the change was made, per the open items); the entry records the intended wiring, and the pi-state entry on local LLM reachability records the still-unverified state.

**See:** pi-state.md — 7caa9c5c-21d2-4480-9058-2d973cd21e2b — as of 2026-10-10

pi-state.md#pi-mounted-at-a-flat-path-no.text:
The container mounts the host's `~/.pi` at a single flat path (currently `/pi`) and points pi at the active profile from there, rather than mounting individual profile subdirectories.

**Reason:** pi's profile directories contain symlinks with relative targets (e.g. a profile's auth file symlinks to a shared location via `../../../agent/...`). Mounting the whole tree at one path keeps those relative links resolving; mounting a profile directory on its own breaks every relative link inside it, because the target directory no longer exists at the relative path.

**Rejected alternative:** mount only the active profile directory. Breaks the internal relative symlinks, so pi would see an incomplete, broken profile.

pi-state.md#pi-extensions-resolve-their-.text:
Pi extensions that live in a profile's extensions or git directories resolve their package imports by walking up the directory tree for a `node_modules` directory.

**Reason:** if the profile root has no `node_modules`, resolution falls through to a globally installed package instead of the version the extension was developed against. On this host the per-extension `node_modules` directories were stale symlinks to homebrew paths that do not exist inside the container, so each extension directory and the profile root needed their own dependency install before pi could load them in the container.

**Consequence:** copying a profile into a container (or a fresh machine) without re-running the per-extension install step produces broken extensions that fail at import time, not at install time.

pi-state.md#local-llm-endpoints-are-unre.text:
Model providers that point at loopback addresses on the host (a local LLM gateway, a local inference server) are not reachable from inside the container: the container's own loopback is not the host's.

**Reason:** container networking isolates loopback; reaching a host service requires the Docker host gateway address (`host.docker.internal`) plus the service's host-side port, and the container's model config predates that.

**Consequence:** cloud-based providers work from the container; host-only LLM endpoints do not until the container's model configuration is pointed at the host gateway address. Recorded as an open item, untested with the gateway running.

repo.md#github-slug-differs-from-the-loc.text:
The project's GitHub repository is named `pi-herdr-docker` while the local working directory and original project name are `pi-agent-docker`.

**Reason:** the public repository was created (or transferred) under the `pi-herdr-docker` slug; the local checkout kept its original name. The two names are both in use in the project's own files, and a future agent searching for one by the other will not find it.

**Consequence:** any automation, link, or documentation that derives the repository name from the directory name (or vice versa) gets the wrong answer. Both names are recorded so the mismatch is a known fact instead of a bug to "fix" one way or the other.

secrets.md#api-keys-are-conditionally-pa.text:
An API key (for a cloud model provider) is passed into the container as an environment variable only when it is set on the host, so the image itself contains no secrets and the container runs with none when the host has none.

**Reason:** baking a key into the image or a committed file would put a live credential in the repository's history or the image registry; passing it per-invocation keeps the image reusable and the credential out of anything that is committed or pushed.

**Rejected alternative:** store the key in a mounted file inside the image build. The key would be in the image layers, readable by anyone who can pull the image, and would have to be rebuilt on every rotation.

**Rejected alternative:** always pass a key (even an empty one). The conditional form makes "no key set" and "key set" visibly different in the container's environment, which matters for debugging which providers are actually reachable.

web-ui.md#web-bridge-is-additive-over-th.text:
The web-UI bridge is built on top of the herdr server image (a second Dockerfile that adds the web component to the same base) and drives the same herdr-state named volume as the plain server container, rather than running a separate herdr instance with its own state.

**Reason:** the browser UI is a second surface over one herdr session, not a second session — attaching from a terminal and from a browser should show the same panes and agents. Building the web image on top of the server image (rather than a parallel image) keeps the two from drifting apart, and reusing the state volume means switching between the two workflows does not lose the working state.

**Rejected alternative:** a separate web container with its own herdr instance and state volume. Two independent herdr sessions for one logical workspace; the user would have to recreate panes/agents in the second one.

**Consequence:** the two workflows (plain server container, web bridge container) are mutually exclusive while running — they share the same state volume, so the web workflow checks that the plain container is not running before starting (and vice versa).
